title: Reverie Moments
tagline: A digital platform built to centralize multi-day event logistics, connecting programs, services, guests, vendors, drivers, and internal teams in one operational system.
summary: A discovery audit of the scope of work for a group-and-crew travel operations platform, and the role research the document was missing.

about: Reverie Moments is a platform designed to centralize multi-day event logistics, bringing programs, services, guests, vendors, drivers, and internal teams into one role-based system. I joined at SOW v0.1 to audit the requirements before implementation, where I identified gaps in the role journeys - most notably the Operations journey, which was still marked WIP despite its responsibility for daily and live OPSKED, service assignments, and real-time execution.

metrics.label: Reduced manual effort
metrics.note: Reduced reliance on paper updates, Excel maintenance and phone-based coordination for day-to-day operations.

metrics.label: Teams connected
metrics.note: GCSM, Operations, Sales, Accounting, Guest Ambassadors, Drivers and Tour Desk brought into one platform.

metrics.label: Less operational workload
metrics.note: Reduced repetitive effort involved in updating services, assignments, statuses and maintaining operational records.

research.intro: The challenge was not a lack of user input — it was that the existing workflow was largely manual. I worked closely with the client through regular calls to understand how their teams planned programs, assigned vendors and drivers, managed daily operations, handled live changes and maintained records. I mapped those real operational needs against the SOW, especially around the Operations workflow, Daily OPSKED and Live OPSKED, and used the gaps and ambiguities in the documentation to guide the product design. The SOW itself identifies the Operations journey as WIP and defines the goal as replacing fragmented manual processes with a centralized system.

methods.name: Client discovery calls
methods.detail: Regular discussions with the client to understand the existing operational process and clarify how work was actually being handled.

methods.name: Existing-process mapping
methods.detail: Mapped the paper, spreadsheet and manual coordination involved in planning and executing services.

methods.name: Operations workflow definition
methods.detail: Focused the design effort on the operational workflows at the heart of the platform, including Daily OPSKED, Live OPSKED, service updates, assignments and issue handling.

methods.name: Vendor & driver coordination
methods.detail: Identified the operational challenge of managing vendor and driver assignments while keeping service status and changes updated in real time.

research.insight: The biggest challenge was the gap between a largely manual operation and the need for faster, more coordinated execution. Through regular discussions with the client, I mapped how teams planned programs, managed services, coordinated vendors and drivers, and handled changes during live operations. This revealed that the Operations team needed a single system to replace scattered spreadsheets, paper-based updates and manual coordination with clearer workflows, real-time visibility and easier control across the entire operation.

painPoints.label: Operations depended on paper and Excel
painPoints.detail: Daily operational work was spread across paper sheets and Excel, with no single digital system to manage services, schedules, vendors, drivers and operational information.

painPoints.label: Excel became difficult to manage at scale
painPoints.detail: As operational information grew, maintaining large Excel-based workflows became cumbersome, making it harder for the team to access and manage information efficiently during day-to-day operations.

painPoints.label: Vendor and driver changes required constant coordination
painPoints.detail: Service assignments, vendor availability, driver coordination and operational changes had to be managed manually, making real-time updates difficult when something changed during execution.

painPoints.label: Changes had limited visibility and accountability
painPoints.detail: Operational updates, service changes, comments and completion details were handled across disconnected processes, making it difficult to maintain a clear record of what changed, when it changed and who handled it. The new requirements specifically called for activity history and audit trails for these actions.

personas.name: Jenny Pearson
personas.quote: My job is to keep every program on schedule and ready to bill - but I only see what’s been published to me, and today none of this is even digital yet.
goals: Carry every program from Active through InProgress to Operated, complete enough for Accounting to bill against.
Hold one accurate source of truth, so client-facing reports match what the team sees internally.
Coordinate vendors and internal assignments across Sales, Tour Desk and Guest Ambassadors without conflicts.
Resolve service and program issues before they reach the client relationship.
frustrations: Day-of visibility is read-only and second-hand: only as good as what OPS publishes, and how promptly.
None of it is digital yet — the coordination this platform is meant to replace happens on paper and in spreadsheets.
No safeguard against double-booking a vendor across overlapping services; availability checking is out of MVP scope.
Vendor has no row in the permission matrix, so there is no rule for what a vendor may do with a ticket assigned to them.

personas.name: Michael Wilson
personas.quote: I’m the one who has to catch problems while they’re still happening in the field - but my own journey through this platform isn’t written down anywhere yet.
goals: Publish a Daily OPSKED accurate enough that every other role can plan their day against it.
Track live execution and catch delays, flight issues and tickets while they are still happening.
Reassign vendors, drivers and Guest Ambassadors quickly when a service breaks, without losing the audit trail.
Resolve or escalate trouble tickets before they reach a guest.
frustrations: The section meant to document this role’s journey is work-in-progress, and describes the Sales team instead.
Ticket status-change and driver-unavailable alerts are described in the functional sections but missing from the notification table.
No availability check exists, so a mid-disruption reassignment can silently collide with an existing commitment.
Offline support is required but undefined: no conflict rule, on the role most likely to be working without signal.

journey.label: Operations, from morning review to day-end rollover

stages.name: Daily review and prep
stages.goal: Get oriented on what is scheduled today, before any plan is published.
stages.actions: Logs in and reviews the Daily Dashboard for all published past and current-day services.
stages.pain: Open question: the SOW describes no OPS-specific review step distinct from the dashboard shared with GCSM.
stages.opportunity: Give Operations a dedicated day view, separate from the shared dashboard.

stages.name: Draft and publish the OPSKED
stages.goal: Produce a schedule the rest of the company can trust once it is published.
stages.actions: In draft: assigns vendors, Guest Ambassadors and service times, moves status from scheduled to in progress, then publishes.
stages.touchpoints: Daily OPSKED, draft and publish views
stages.pain: Billing fields OPS is expected to enter conflict with §1.9, which grants OPS no billing access at all.
stages.opportunity: Resolve the billing-permission contradiction before build, and add a lightweight vendor-conflict warning.
stages.emotion: Focused, mildly anxious — publishing locks the schedule

stages.name: Live execution monitoring
stages.goal: Catch delays, flight issues and status changes as they happen.
stages.actions: Monitors Live OPSKED service cards, works status filters and reminder timers, expands cards for detail.
stages.touchpoints: Live OPSKED dashboard, service cards, timers
stages.pain: No vendor availability check in MVP scope — a reassignment can silently double-book.
stages.opportunity: Add a real-time availability check as a flag, not a hard block.

stages.name: Issue and exception handling
stages.goal: Resolve disruptions before they reach the guest or the client.
stages.actions: Creates and progresses trouble tickets, tracks flight delays, combines and uncombines linked services, reassigns vendors and drivers.
stages.touchpoints: Trouble ticket module, reassignment UI, flight delay indicators
stages.pain: Auto-assignment rules are unresolved by the client, and ticket status-change notifications are missing from the consolidated table.
stages.opportunity: Finalise the auto-assignment rules, and add ticket-status alerts to the notification spec.

stages.name: Guest and vendor coordination
stages.goal: Keep vendor, driver and Guest Ambassador assignments conflict-free through the day.
stages.actions: Oversees check-in and checkout activity on service cards, confirms vendor task status.
stages.touchpoints: Live OPSKED guest check-in data, vendor assignments panel
stages.pain: Vendor has no defined permissions row, despite being granted ticket-transition rights in the narrative.
stages.opportunity: Define Vendor as a first-class role, or document OPS acting on a vendor’s behalf.

stages.name: Day-end closeout and rollover
stages.goal: Close the day with nothing silently dropped.
stages.actions: Reviews the automatic 23:59 export and confirms which services roll forward to tomorrow.
stages.touchpoints: Live OPSKED end-of-day export, next-day carryover
stages.pain: Offline and local sync has no documented conflict handling — the risk lands on low-connectivity field work.
stages.opportunity: Document offline conflict resolution before mobile access ships.
stages.emotion: Relieved but incomplete — unresolved items roll forward

solutions.name: A single digital workspace for operations
solutions.resolves: Daily operations depended on paper and heavy spreadsheets
solutions.detail: Replaced fragmented paper and spreadsheet-based work with one platform for managing programs, services, employees, vendors, drivers and operational records in one place.

solutions.name: Daily & Live OPSKED as the operational control centre
solutions.resolves: Daily and live operations required constant manual updates and coordination
solutions.detail: Brought daily schedules and live service execution into one workspace, allowing OPS to update service status, assignments, delays and operational changes directly instead of relying on paper updates and repeated calls.

solutions.name: Real-time vendor & driver coordination
solutions.detail: Connected vendor and driver assignments directly to service operations, making changes visible within the platform and giving the team a faster way to manage disruptions, reassignments and ongoing services.

solutions.name: One source of truth for operational records
solutions.resolves: Operational information was scattered, making reporting and tracking difficult
solutions.detail: Centralized employees, vendors, drivers, services and transactions, with reporting capabilities that made operational information easier to maintain, review and turn into custom reports.

visualDesign.statement: Before designing the interface, I turned the complex operational requirements into a visual system of journeys, flows, roles, and problem–solution mappings. These artefacts made the product logic easier to validate with the client, exposed gaps early, and gave the development team a clear foundation for translating operational processes into the platform.

title: APTEN
tagline: A structured RFP replaces cold-calling warehouses and the trust gap that comes with it.
summary: A B2B marketplace that turns 3PL selection into a structured, evidenced process.
about: APTEN is a B2B marketplace that connects brands and manufacturers with third-party logistics providers through a structured RFP process. Instead of brands cold-calling warehouses, the platform handles the whole path — profile and volume data intake, algorithmic matching, long list to short list curation, a shared Data Room for evaluation, proposal comparison, and final award and onboarding.

metrics.label: User roles designed end-to-end
metrics.note: Brand, 3PL Provider, and Consultant — each with its own dashboard, journey, and permission set, not one generic flow stretched three ways.

metrics.label: Point trust gap identified
metrics.note: The gap between 3PL self-rated success and customer experience, found in research — and the exact distrust this design was built to close.

metrics.label: Research findings mapped to real screens
metrics.note: Every opportunity tied to a specific flow — Volume Profile, Data Room, Cost Summary, Fulfillment Contract — not a general recommendation.

research.intro: Desk research against genuine user-generated content and formal industry data, not assumption. Every claim below is traceable to a named source; where evidence was a single anecdote, it is labelled as one rather than generalised.

methods.name: Merchant forum mining
methods.detail: Shopify Community threads where brands describe 3PL billing and fulfilment failures in their own words.

methods.name: Formal industry survey
methods.detail: SCALA UK survey via Fleet News — 20% of UK companies report difficulties with their 3PL.

methods.name: Specialist consultancy analysis
methods.detail: Staci Americas and Fulfillrite on how 3PL RFPs are actually run, and the red flags brands miss.

methods.name: Verified review teardown
methods.detail: G2 reviews of Clutch and Freightos, read for distrust of the matching platforms themselves.

research.insight: Only 35% of customers agree with the 54% of 3PLs who rate their own performance as highly successful — a 19-point gap between what is claimed and what is experienced.
research.insightAttribution: SCALA UK industry survey, via Fleet News

painPoints.label: Rates move after you commit
painPoints.detail: Quoted pricing changes once inventory and money are already in. Documented cases moved $10 to $14.50 per order and $8 to $25 per label.
painPoints.evidence: Practical Ecommerce (Beardbrand); Shopify Community; Fulfillrite — Theme 1, high severity, three independent sources.

painPoints.label: Capability is indistinguishable from sales talk
painPoints.detail: Brands cannot separate real operational capacity from a team that says yes to everything, and there is no verified data to check it against before signing.
painPoints.evidence: SCALA/Fleet News UK survey; Fulfillrite red-flags analysis — Theme 2, high severity.

painPoints.label: The RFP is rushed and shallow
painPoints.detail: RFPs get launched reactively as a fix to an existing crisis, sent to too many vendors without pre-filtering, and without the operational data needed to price accurately.
painPoints.evidence: Staci Americas — Theme 3, recurring pattern across client engagements.

painPoints.label: The matching platforms are themselves distrusted
painPoints.detail: Reviewers report pay-for-placement undermining "verified" review claims, and platform fees that only surface at checkout.
painPoints.evidence: G2 reviews of Clutch.co and Freightos — Theme 6, formal review data.

matrix.caption: Where APTEN sits against the incumbents

competitors.name: Fulfill.com
competitors.verdict: Algorithmic matching plus human consultation, but fully form-gated with no RFP mechanism, no document exchange and a 3–5 day turnaround.

competitors.name: WarehousingAndFulfillment.com
competitors.verdict: Twenty years of curation and an 8% provider approval rate, wrapped in a basic UI with no proposal management and no transparency on how matching works.

competitors.name: Clutch.co
competitors.verdict: The most mature verified-review infrastructure in B2B services — undermined, per its own reviewers, by paid placement.

competitiveAudit.whitespace: Every incumbent stops at the introduction. None of them owns the evaluation — no shared document room, no structured proposal comparison, no contract record that holds after signing. That gap is exactly where the documented harm happens.

personas.name: Alex William
personas.quote: I can’t expect a fulfillment partner to care about my brand as much as I do every single day.
goals: Find a 3PL that genuinely fits their volume and SKU profile without weeks of unstructured comparison.
Lock in pricing and SLA terms that will not change after signing.
See real operational performance data before committing, not just sales claims.
frustrations: A quoted rate changed materially after signing — real cases moved $10 to $14.50 per order.
Hard to tell real capability from a sales team that says yes to everything.
No pre-commitment visibility into performance, against a measured 19-point claim-versus-experience gap.

personas.name: Jemmy Anderson
personas.quote: Generic pitches about warehouse locations and carrier relationships won’t win business anymore.
goals: Be matched with brands whose volume genuinely fits operational capacity, instead of chasing poor-fit prospects.
Differentiate on real operational outcomes rather than generic infrastructure claims.
Trust that platform fees are transparent and tied to genuinely qualified leads.
frustrations: The average 3PL sale needs six to eight touchpoints, but most reps give up after two or three.
Consultant and agency referral channels are underused across the industry.
Suspicion that competitors can buy visibility rather than earn it.

journey.label: The brand user, from first search to signed contract

stages.name: Awareness
stages.goal: Recognise that the current fulfilment approach will not survive their order volume.
stages.actions: Searches online, asks peers for referrals — often already mid-crisis with the incumbent.
stages.touchpoints: Search results, industry blogs, word of mouth, competitor directories
stages.pain: RFPs get triggered reactively, in response to an active problem, never planned.
stages.opportunity: Speak directly to the reactive-search moment; help a rushed brand define real requirements before comparing anyone.

stages.name: Consideration
stages.goal: Decide whether APTEN is a trustworthy way to find a 3PL at all.
stages.actions: Weighs the value proposition against a manual search and the incumbent platforms.
stages.pain: Matching platforms carry documented distrust; a 19-point claim-versus-experience gap sits behind it.
stages.opportunity: Surface trust signals early — transparent deposit framing, evidence that matches are not pay-to-play.

stages.name: Onboarding & setup
stages.goal: Get business profile and operational data into the platform accurately.
stages.actions: Signs up, completes the business profile, uploads order history, builds the product catalog.
stages.touchpoints: Sign-up, onboarding wizard, Profile module, five-step Volume Profile
stages.pain: Gathering detailed operational history takes real time, but pricing accuracy later depends on it.
stages.opportunity: Reinforce graceful degradation — the "insufficient data" fallback belongs throughout onboarding, not only in the Data Room.

stages.name: Define requirements
stages.goal: Get matched with 3PLs that genuinely fit, without months of vetting.
stages.actions: Selects services, sets locations and budget, reviews the RFP dashboard and its matches.
stages.touchpoints: Define Requirements screen, RFP dashboard, Define Scope wizard, 3PL profiles
stages.pain: The matching logic is unspecified — the brand has no visibility into why a given 3PL surfaced.
stages.opportunity: Highest-leverage point to close the trust gap: even a lightweight "why this match" tied to Volume Profile data.

stages.name: Engagement & evaluation
stages.goal: Verify a shortlisted 3PL’s claims before committing money and inventory.
stages.actions: Invites 3PLs into the Data Room, reads documents, asks questions, compares proposals.
stages.touchpoints: Data Room, FAQ and Q&A, Ask a Question modal, proposal review
stages.pain: Quoted rates have moved after signing — $10 to $14.50 per order, $8 to $25 per label.
stages.opportunity: Resolve the open question in favour of server-side Cost Summary calculation — it closes a documented harm.

stages.name: Award & handoff
stages.goal: Formalise the partnership, confident the terms will hold.
stages.actions: Names a finalist, awards the winner, begins the Fulfilment Contract wizard.
stages.touchpoints: Award action, Fulfilment Contract wizard, Relationships kanban
stages.pain: This is exactly where documented cases show terms changing between agreement and execution.
stages.opportunity: Make the locked, platform-tracked contract record a headline value proposition, not a quiet backend detail.

solutions.name: Server-side Cost Summary and a locking contract wizard
solutions.detail: Cost is calculated server-side and the Fulfilment Contract wizard locks terms to match the Data Room proposal exactly. Post-signing changes require a logged, visible Change Request.

solutions.name: Mandatory, verified Performance Metrics
solutions.resolves: Capability is indistinguishable from sales talk
solutions.detail: A 3PL cannot receive RFP invitations until dispatch time, order accuracy and return processing are filled in and admin-verified, and they must be refreshed on a cadence so the data stays current.

solutions.name: A staged, pre-checked RFP flow
solutions.resolves: The RFP is rushed and shallow
solutions.detail: Define Scope, then Long List, then Short List — with a structured pre-RFP checklist that nudges order-history and volume data to completion before the brand can proceed.

solutions.name: Transparency as a first-class feature
solutions.resolves: The matching platforms are themselves distrusted
solutions.detail: A plain-language "how matching works" explainer, a "why this match" note tied to Volume Profile data on every suggestion, and the $100 deposit and 3PL billing model stated in full before signup.

visualDesign.statement: The visual language was designed to make complex procurement decisions feel clear, structured, and trustworthy. A restrained interface, strong hierarchy, and data-forward layouts help users quickly evaluate providers, compare proposals, track progress, and make high-consequence decisions without unnecessary visual noise.
